## Introduction

The sinoatrial node is the heart's primary pacemaker and, therefore, a crucial component of the heart's conduction system. In an average adult, the crescent-shaped sinoatrial node is approximately 13.5 mm long, receives innervation from the vagus and sympathetic nerves, and is located subepicardially. The sinoatrial nodal artery supplies blood to the sinoatrial node and branches from the right coronary artery in 60% of cases and from the left circumflex coronary artery in 40% of cases.

Sinus bradycardia is a cardiac rhythm in which the sinus node initiates cardiac muscle depolarization, but the heart rate is slower. Traditionally, a heart rate less than 60 beats per minute was classified as bradycardia. However, the 2025 Americcan Heart Association Advanced Cardiac Life Support update defines clinically meaningful bradycardia as a heart rate below 50 beats per minute. The diagnosis of sinus bradycardia requires an electrocardiogram demonstrating a normal sinus rhythm at a rate less than 50 bpm (see Image. Sinus Bradycardia). A normal sinus rhythm meets the following criteria:

Regular rhythm, with a P wave preceding every QRS complex

The P wave is upright in leads I and II; the P wave is biphasic in lead V1

The maximum amplitude of a P wave is less than or equal to 2.5 mm in leads II and III

The rate is between 50 bpm and 100 bpm

The following are definitions of different types of sinus node dysfunction:

Sinus bradycardia: Sinus rate < 50 bpm

Ectopic atrial bradycardia: Atrial depolarization from an atrial pacemaker other than the sinus node. Rate is < 50

Sinoatrial exit block: Blocked conduction betwen the sinus node and the atrial tissue. Electrocardiogram (ECG) may show group beating and sinus pauses

Sinus pause: Sinus node depolarizes > 3 seconds after atrial depolarization

Sinus node arrest: Sinus node depolarization is absent

Tachycardia-bradycardia syndrome: Periods of atrial tachycardia, atrial flutter, or atrial fibrillation mixed with sinus bradycardia, ectopic atrial bradycardia, or sinus pausing

Chronotropic incompetence: Inability to incease heart rate with increased activity or demand

Isorhythmic dissociation: Atrial depolarization that is slower than ventricular depolarization

## Etiology

Sinus bradycardia has many intrinsic and extrinsic etiologies:

Intrinsic Etiologies

Chest trauma

Ischemic heart disease (acute myocardial infarction and chronic coronary artery disease)

Repair of congenital heart disease

Sick sinus syndrome

Radiation therapy

Amyloidosis

Pericarditis

Lyme disease

Rheumatic fever

Collagen vascular disease

Myocarditis

Neuromuscular disorders, including X-linked muscular dystrophy

Familial disorders

Inherited channelopathies ]

Extrinsic Etiologies

Vasovagal stimulation (eg, endotracheal suctioning)

Carotid sinus hypersensitivity

β-Blockers

Calcium channel blockers

Digoxin

Ivabradine

Clonidine

Reserpine

Adenosine

Cimetidine

Antiarrhythmic drugs (classes I-IV)

Lithium

Amitriptyline

Opiods

Cannabinoids

Hypothyroidism

Sleep apnea

Hypoxia

Intracranial hypertension

Hyperkalemia

Iatrogenic (eg, ablation or valve surgery)

Anorexia nervosa

## Pathophysiology

Sinus bradycardia, similar to other bradyarrhythmias, is caused by a multitude of intrinsic and extrinsic factors that may compromise the integrity of the sinus node. These factors can cause failure of impulse formation in the sinoatrial node, the atrioventricular node, or the His-Purkinje system. Sinus bradycardia is an incidental finding in many healthy adults, including athletes, and during sleep. Athletes have physiologic sinus bradycardia due to increased vagal tone. Conversely, sinus bradycardia is common in sick sinus syndrome, which involves dysfunction of the sinoatrial node. Pathologic sinus bradycardia is more common in older adults with concomitant heart disease.

The pathophysiology of sinoatrial node dysfunction is usually due to electrophysiological and structural remodeling of the node. The specialized myocytes in the node are surrounded by connective tissue that insulates the node, a structural framework that protects the area from hyperpolarization of adjacent myocytes. The collagen content of this area increases with age, resulting in increased fibrosis and slower conduction.

## History and Physical

Most patients with sinus bradycardia are asymptomatic. Healthy young adults and athletes tend to have increased vagal tone and sinus bradycardia at rest. In addition, patients aged 65 years or older may develop sinus bradycardia during sleep due to age-related changes in the sinoatrial node. The patient's history helps correlate symptoms with sinus bradycardia on electrocardiography, aiding accurate diagnosis.

Patients with symptoms may experience fatigue, exercise intolerance, lightheadedness, dizziness, syncope or presyncope, worsening of anginal symptoms, worsening congestive heart failure, or cognitive changes. Important elements of the patient history include recent medication changes, medication overdose, chest pain, shortness of breath, prior myocardial infarction, intermittent palpitations, chest trauma, rash or recent tick bite, current or prior streptococcal pharyngitis, family history of sinus bradycardia, and family history of muscular dystrophy. Moreover, physical examination findings should be interpreted in the context of the patient's history to help narrow the differential diagnosis (eg, heart murmurs or skin examination findings suggestive of a developing rash).

The physical examination may reveal the following:

Cyanosis

Peripheral edema

Altered mental status

Dyspnea

Rales and crackles
